vertebra and vertebrae get arthritic.
The joint between C1 and C2 takes more
rotation than any other joint in the
neck.
Decades of that wear thin the cartilage.
The body responds by laying down extra
bone at the edges, small spurs called
osteophytes. A spur that grows into a
ring narrows the ring. A spur at the top
joint changes the shape of the loop the
artery has to make. The bow hunter case
reports keep describing a bony spur or
an arthritic top joint as the thing
doing the pinching.
The young neck rotates and the artery
has slack.
The old neck rotates and the artery has
a spur waiting for it.
The second is the artery wall. A
vertebral artery at 30 is elastic. Turn
the head and it stretches, kinks a
little, and springs back.
With age, the wall stiffens and
thickens. The same turn that used to
bend a hose now folds a pipe. A stiffer
artery is easier to pinch closed and
slower to reopen.
It is also more likely to tear at the
inner lining under a hard stretch.
That tear is the dissection the salon
literature describes, and I will get to
the salon.
The third is plaque. Atherosclerosis
does not deposit evenly.
Over years, one vertebral artery often
ends up narrower than the other, and the
brain quietly shifts its supply to the
wider one. That is how a person arrives
at 70 with a dominant artery and a spare
that cannot carry the load.
The StatPearls definition turns on that
word, dominant.
If the artery that gets pinched is the
spare, nothing happens and nobody ever
knows.
Pause.
If it is the dominant one, there is no
reserve. Put the three together, a
narrower ring, a stiffer vessel, and one
side doing all the work.
None of that is a disease. It is
ordinary aging,
but it means the rare syndrome sits at
the bottom of a slope, and everyone over
50 is standing somewhere on that slope.
The same turn on the same pillow has a
different margin every decade.
MedlinePlus, the National Library of
Medicine's public encyclopedia,
list what a starved vertebrobasilar
system feels like. Vertigo, the room
spinning, blurred or double vision,
slurred speech, trouble swallowing,
numbness, sudden weakness, loss of
coordination, and in the worst cases, a
drop attack where the legs simply give
out.
Read that list against Walter's kitchen
sink.
Read it against the ceiling that slid to
the right in the dark before dawn.
If a channel that reads the papers and
hands you the questions is worth
something to you, subscribe.
That is how you make sure it keeps
showing up. And now put the neck in the
position most people put it in for 7
hours a night.
Now take each pillow mistake in turn and
watch what it does to those two
arteries.
Too low on your side, the Walter pillow.
Your head drops toward the mattress and
the neck bends sideways toward the down
shoulder. And because a bent neck will
not stay purely bent, the head also
rotates, chin drifting toward the
mattress.
That is side bending plus rotation held
all night.
It is a gentler version of the angle the
angio CT caught.
Too high on your side, the two pillow
stack.
Now the head is pushed up and away from
the down shoulder.
The neck bends the other direction and
the same rotation creeps in from the
other side.
Too high on your back, the chin drives
toward the chest.
This one is mostly a muscle and
breathing problem and it narrows the
airway.
But I mention it because the fix people
reach for, throwing the pillows off and
sleeping flat,
produces the next one.
Too low on your back or no pillow at
all, the head drops back, the chin
points at the ceiling, the throat opens.
That is hyperextension
and hyperextension has its own
literature from a very different room.
A recent scoping review in the emergency
medicine literature gathered the
published cases of what the authors call
beauty parlor stroke syndrome.
The pattern is a person, most often
older, most often a woman, leaning back
over a salon shampoo basin. The neck is
bent backward over the hard rim while
their hair is washed. In the days
afterwards, some of them develop
dizziness, vision problems, and in a
subset, a confirmed stroke in the
vertebral basilar territory.
The proposed mechanism is the same
artery. This time stretched and
compressed by extension rather than
rotation.
In some cases, the inner wall of the
artery tears, a dissection, and a clot
forms on the tear.
The review is careful. It calls these
case reports. It does not give you a
rate, and neither will I.
What it does establish is narrower and
more useful. A neck angle held for the
length of a shampoo has been documented
to injure this artery in susceptible
people.
A shampoo is 10 minutes. A pillow is 7
hours. Nobody has run the trial that
would settle this directly.
I want to be careful here, because this
is not a video that claims your pillow
is going to kill you. Most strokes are
never traced to a pillow, and I am not
going to trace them to one.
There is no study in which 1,000 older
adults were randomized to good pillows
and bad pillows and followed for
strokes.
I will not pretend there is.
What the record contains is the
mechanism, proven on dynamic scans.
It contains the hairdresser's chair as a
natural experiment in extension. And
then one more piece, which is the clock.
A circadian analysis of a stroke trial
called FAST-MAG charted when patients'
strokes began across the 24-hour cycle.
The authors separated ischemic strokes,
the clot kind, from hemorrhagic strokes,
the bleed kind. And they separated
strokes that started while the patient
was awake from strokes that the patient
woke up with.
Wake-up stroke is its own category in
this research. The person goes to sleep
normal and opens their eyes with a weak
arm or slurred tongue.
Nobody can say when in the night it
started. That matters for more than the
research. The clot-dissolving drugs run
on a clock that starts at onset. And a
wake-up stroke has no known onset. The
clot starts from the last moment the
person was seen well, which is the
moment they went to bed.
Pause.
Hours of that window are gone before
anyone wakes up.
A Romanian hospital study asked the same
question, whether stroke onset has a
daily rhythm. Enlisting the possible
outside influences, it named the
sleep-wake cycle and the act of rising
into an upright position.
Rising, the moment Walter's episodes
were most reliable.
What the clock proves, the morning surge
in blood pressure,
the overnight thickening of the blood,
the dehydration of a night without
water.
The first two are established
contributors to the early morning stroke
pattern.
The dehydration is often cited. Posture
is a candidate on the list, not a
convicted cause.
But hold the pieces side by side, an
artery that closes with rotation,
a neck that a bad pillow rotates for
hours, a stroke pattern that clusters
around waking and rising, and a scan
taken later that morning with the head
straight that shows nothing.
Pause.
That is why this channel is talking
about a pillow.
Now, three more people from the pattern,
because Walter is only one of the shapes
this takes. The headache is there at
6:00 and gone by 10.
Dolores is 66, Tucson, Arizona, and she
sleeps on her back.
Three years ago, her doctor mentioned
acid reflux and she started propping
herself on two pillows, then three.
Her chin now sleeps on her chest.
What she notices is not vertigo. It is
that headache at the base of the skull
every morning fading by midmorning.
And a strange heaviness in her arms when
she reaches into a high cupboard.
The muscles at the back of her neck have
been stretched for 7 hours a night and
the nerves through them are unhappy.
The small muscles under the skull, the
ones that hold the head level, have been
on a stretch all night. They tighten to
protect themselves and tight muscles
there refer pain to the back of the
head.
But the part that matters for this video
is her fix.
Some mornings the headache is bad enough
that she pulls all the pillows off.
She sleeps flat on her back with her
head tipped back, the shampoo basin
position, for the last 2 hours before
dawn.
The correct answer for Dolores is
neither three pillows nor zero.
It is one pillow of about 2 to 3 inches
compressed.
And here is the one thing the news
coverage of pillows never gets to
because it is buried in the
rehabilitation literature.
The advice Dolores was given, "Prop your
head up for reflux," is advice written
for the stomach.
Nobody was thinking about the neck when
they gave it.
Every pillow she adds lifts the head
alone and leaves the shoulders flat on
the mattress.
That is a fold and the fold is at the
neck.
The underreported fix is to tilt the
whole bed instead.
Risers under the two legs at the head of
the frame raise the mattress as a single
slope. The head, the neck, the
shoulders, and the chest all go up
together at the same angle.
Nothing bends. The chin stays level and
the throat stays neutral on one ordinary
pillow of the right height.
That way the neck stays straight and the
torso does the tilting.
It is not a product, it is not a gadget,
and it does not show up in a headline.
It is a pair of blocks under a bed frame
and it takes the question off the neck
entirely.
Reflux is something to raise with her
own doctor. The neck angle is something
she can fix tonight. The ringing is
loudest before his feet hit the floor.
Ray is 74, Baltimore, a side sleeper on
a pillow his son bought him in 2016.
It has lost half its height. The ringing
is in his left ear and it fades as the
morning goes on.
There is also a lurch, a half second of
the room swinging, when he turns to look
at the passenger seat.
He has been told it is his age and
possibly his ears. It may well be his
ears. Tinnitus has many causes and most
of them are in the ear, not the artery.
But the timing, worst on waking, and the
trigger, turning the head, are exactly
the two features the vertebrobasilar
literature keeps flagging.
The inner ear draws its blood from the
same vertebrobasilar system, which is
why the MedlinePlus list includes it.
And the one thing Ray can change without
a prescription is the 4 in his head has
been dropping every night.
Ray's correct height is his
shoulder-to-neck measurement on him,
about 5 in compressed, in a pillow firm
enough to hold that height until
morning.
Marlene is 68, Sacramento, and she has
slept on her stomach since she was a
girl.
To breathe on your stomach, you must
turn your head to the side and not a
little. 90°.
The full bow hunter turn, the angle the
angio CT was taken at, held for as long
as she sleeps.
She is fit, her blood pressure is good,
and she has never had a dizzy spell.
That is worth saying because most
stomach sleepers never do.
The vertebral arteries in most people
have enough slack and enough backup to
tolerate it.
The concern is what happens as a person
ages into a narrowed artery, a dominant
side, and arthritic top joint.
The tolerance quietly runs out while the
habit stays the same.
What Marlene needs is not a different
pillow.
It is a position, and it [clears throat]
is the hardest one on the list.
So, what to do in the order that matters
most, starting tonight. First, measure.
Do the wall test I described, shoulder
against the wall, measure wall to the
side of the neck under the ear, subtract
about an inch,
then lie on your side on your current
pillow and have someone take a
photograph from the foot of the bed,
or prop your phone on the dresser and
use the timer.
Look at the line from your nose down to
the center of your chest.
If it bends toward the mattress, the
pillow is too low.
If it bends toward the ceiling, too
high.
The photograph is the real test. The
tape measure only gets you into the
right range. And if the two disagree,
believe the picture.
This takes 4 minutes, and it answers the
question that the brightly lit scan
cannot.
Second, retire the pancake in the stack.
Replace with one pillow that holds your
measured height when compressed,
and test it by lying on it 10 minutes,
not squeezing it in the aisle.
The filling decides whether that height
is still there at dawn. So, here is the
short version.
In the materials testing I have read,
latex holds its compressed height best
night after night for years. Shredded
foam comes second, and you can open the
cover and add or remove handfuls until
the height is right.
Or build the layers yourself. Thin
inserts inside a cover, and pull one out
if you tend to end the night on your
back.
Down and polyfill feel wonderful at 10
and flatten by two. So, if you love
down, measure it compressed, not
fluffed.
Next firm is not one number. A 200-lb
sleeper compresses a pillow far more
than a 130-lb sleeper. So, the heavier
shoulder needs denser fill or more of
it. Buy for your weight, not for the
label. Then give it three nights. A
correct height will feel wrong at first.
A stiff neck, tightness across the
shoulder, maybe a restless hour.
Pause.
That is not the pillow failing. That is
your neck meeting a position it is not
held for years.
Do not revert to the pancake on night
two.
Hold through night three, judge on night
four.
Third, if you sleep on your stomach,
begin the slow move to your side. Nobody
changes a 60-year habit in a night. The
method that tends to hold is a body
pillow, a long one.
Hug it along the front so the top knee
and top arm have somewhere to rest.
That lets a stomach sleeper lie mostly
on the side with a slight forward lean.
It keeps the head at perhaps 20° of
rotation instead of 90.
20 is not zero. It is a great deal less
than 90.
Fourth, change how you get up. The
Romanian hospital study named rising
into an upright position as a suspect in
the morning stroke pattern.
The blood pressure literature agrees
that the first minute upright is a
vulnerable one for older adults.
So, sit on the edge of the bed for a
slow count of 60 before you stand.
Do not throw the covers off and lunge
for the bathroom.
Let the vertebral arteries, which have
been bent for 7 hours, unbend and let
the blood pressure settle. It costs 1
minute. Fifth, do the seated turn test
and do it carefully.
Sit in a firm chair, feet flat, someone
in the room.
Slowly turn your head to the left as far
as it comfortably goes and hold it for
10 seconds.
Come back to center.
Rest.
Then the right.
What you are looking for is anything
from the MedlinePlus list. Dizziness,
the room shifting, blurred or doubled
vision, a wave of nausea, ringing that
starts or changes, tingling in the face
or hands.
If any of that shows up on rotation and
stops when you face forward again,
that is not something to fix with a
pillow. Pause.
That is a pattern to describe in exactly
those words to your physician. A doctor
who hears symptoms provoked by turning
the head has a reason to order the
dynamic scan rather than the ordinary
one.
And if you already have those symptoms
without the test, stop the test and make
the call.
This is educational. It is not a
diagnosis and the person on the screen
is not your doctor.
The words decide the scan, so this is
exactly what to say when you get there.
Four sentences. One,
my symptoms start when I turn my head
and I can name the direction.
Two, they stop when I bring my head back
to straight. Three, they are worse in
the first 10 minutes after I get up in
the morning.
Four, I sleep on my side on a pillow
that compresses to about 2 inches and I
have for years.
Fill in your own direction and your own
inches.
Write them on an index card and read
them if you have to.
Those four sentences are not a
diagnosis. They are a description of a
provoked, reversible, position-dependent
symptom,
which is the language of the bow hunter
literature.
A doctor who hears dizzy will think
inner ear, and most of the time they
will be right.
A doctor who hears dizzy only on
rotation, resolves it straight, has a
different list.
That list includes the vertebral artery,
and the standard test of that artery at
rest will not answer the question
what you can expect.
The first study is usually a Doppler
ultrasound of the neck. A probe along
the side listening to flow in the
vertebral artery.
In the dynamic version, they measure
head straight, then turned each way.
Flow that drops on the turn and recovers
at straight is the finding.
If ultrasound is unclear, next is a CT
angiogram. The European Spine Journal
scan,
dye in a vein, one picture head
straight, one turned.
That head turned image is the point. So,
if nobody asked you to turn your head,
ask whether the study was dynamic.
Sixth, and this one is not about the
pillow at all, know the FAST check.
The Centers for Disease Control teaches
four letters, F.A.S.T.
Face. Ask the person to smile and watch
for a droop on one side.
Arms. Ask them to raise both and watch
for one drifting down. Speech. Ask them
to repeat a simple sentence and listen
for slurring.
Time. If any of those are present, call
911 immediately and note the time you
first saw it. The treatments that
reverse a clot are measured in minutes
from onset.
The vertebrobasilar strokes we have been
discussing are the ones that sometimes
do not show a drooping face.
They show as sudden vertigo, a sudden
loss of balance, sudden double vision, a
sudden inability to walk straight. The
CDC lists sudden trouble walking,
dizziness, and loss of coordination
among the warning signs alongside the
face and arm signs.
Treat those as the same emergency.
Do not wait to see if it passes. And if
you have vertigo, double vision, or
weakness that came on suddenly,
this is not the moment for a pillow.
Pause.
It is the moment for the phone.
Put it in order.
There are two arteries at the back of
your neck threaded through the bones
with a hairpin turn at the top.
The European Spine Journal review showed
on a dynamic scan that when the top
joint rotates, the artery closes.
Every night a pillow 2 in too low or 3
too high sets the neck into a milder
version and holds it till morning.
The fix is not a supplement and not a
surgery. It is a measurement. One firm
pillow at that height, a slow migration
off the stomach, 60 seconds on the edge
of the bed,
and the seated turn test carried to your
own physician.
Walter, the composite, was told his
scans were clean. And they were in the
position they were taken in.
The question that would have caught it
was the one nobody was paid to ask.
What happens when you turn your head?
And what have you been sleeping on?
That is the question this channel exists
to put in your hands.
Nothing here replaces the judgment of a
doctor who can examine you.
If this reached you, send it to the side
sleeper in your family who has had the
same flat pillow since the last decade.
Pause.
Because the measurement takes 4 minutes
and the ceiling should not move before
the sun is up.
Pause.
And if you want the next paper we read
to land in your feed, hit like and
subscribe.

records.channelDescription:
Clear, research-backed health answers for adults over 60.

Dr. Vitalis takes the questions older adults actually face and explains what the evidence says in plain language. Examples: a blood pressure reading that looks "normal" but isn't, legs that feel weaker on the stairs, a common pill with side effects nobody mentioned, a warning sign that's easy to blame on age.

What we cover:
• Blood pressure, heart health and stroke warning signs
• Kidneys, blood sugar and circulation
• Leg strength, balance and preventing falls
• Medications and supplements worth asking your doctor about
• Everyday food choices, without the hype

Every video ends with simple next steps: what to watch for, what to ask at your next appointment, and when to call right away.

Subscribe for the next one.

For educational purposes only. Not medical advice. Always talk with your own doctor before changing medications or treatment. If you think you're having a stroke or heart attack, call 911.

records.text:
After 80, the room tilting when you stand isn't getting up too fast. It's one of 5 body changes a 12-minute visit never covers. Muscle that goes faster than it used to, a thirst that stops speaking up, pills that land harder than they did at 60, a blood pressure that lags behind you when you stand, and a night's sleep that breaks into pieces. For each one: what is ordinary, what is a warning sign, and the single habit that helps most.

The eighties bring a set of changes that are not disease, but are not nothing either. Sarcopenia — age-related muscle loss — speeds up. The thirst signal weakens, so dehydration shows up as a morning headache, dizziness or sudden confusion instead of thirst. Medication sensitivity rises, so the same dose does more. Baroreflex sensitivity slows, producing orthostatic hypotension, the lying-to-standing drop that drives falls. And sleep timing shifts earlier with more night waking. We follow Howard, 83, a composite built from published case reports, through all five, from the first glass of water to the brown-bag medication review and the standing blood pressure reading that changed his prescriptions.

⏱ CHAPTERS
0:00 — The half-second the room doesn't come with you
0:46 — Straight up or sit: answer before you watch
1:07 — Howard, 83: fine, and quietly not fine
8:04 — Change #5: the muscle loss blamed on everything else
13:16 — Change #4: the thirst that stopped speaking up
15:53 — Why first-morning urine color tells you how the night went
17:44 — Change #3: seven pills landing harder at 80
19:14 — Change #2: sleep that breaks into pieces by 4:40
23:05 — Change #1: the blood pressure that lags when you stand
29:57 — Howard's 24-point drop and what his doctor changed
30:34 — The brown bag, the chair stands, and the 911 list
31:09 — Tonight: the glass of water on the nightstand

Tell me in the comments, two words only: when you get out of bed, do you stand straight up or sit first? If you want the next change explained before it finds you, subscribe and send this to the one person in your family who still says they just got up too fast.

⚠️ DISCLAIMER
This video is for educational purposes only and does not constitute medical advice. Howard and every person described in this video are composites drawn from published case reports, not real patients. Nobody on this channel is a licensed physician, and the visuals in this video are AI-generated. Consult your own doctor before changing any medication, fluid intake, exercise routine or sleep aid, and ask them for lying and standing blood pressure readings at your next visit. A faint, a fall that strikes your head (especially on a blood thinner), chest pain, a weak face or arm, or slurred speech is an emergency: call 911, do not wait for an appointment.

6:50 in the morning.
You push up out of the kitchen chair and
for one long second the room has not
come with you.
The counter slides a little to the left
and your hand finds the table edge on
its own.
Then everything settles and you tell
yourself you simply got up too fast.
At 80, you did not get up too fast. Your
body got slow at something it used to do
in a quarter of a second.
That slowness is one of five changes
that tend to arrive in the 80s and
almost nobody sits you down and explains
them.
Five of them. For each, what is
ordinary, what is a warning, and the one
habit that helps most.
One of these five is in a different
league from the others. It is the one
you just felt in that chair and it comes
last.
So, answer this for yourself.
When you get out of bed in the morning,
do you stand straight up or do you sit
on the edge of the mattress first?
Two words. Straight up or sit.
Tell me in the comments, just those two
words and keep your answer.
The last change on this list is going to
tell you exactly what it means.
Howard is 83. Howard, like everyone you
will meet here, is a composite drawn
from real case reports.
He lives alone in a two-bedroom ranch
house outside Dayton.
>> [clears throat]
>> If you asked him how he was doing, he
would say fine and he would mostly mean
it.
He is in bed by 9:00 and awake at 4:40
whether he likes it or not.
He takes seven pills with a cup of
coffee, then a second cup, and nothing
else to drink until lunch.
His left hand gave up on the jar of
pickles last month. Now he runs the lid
under hot water and uses the rubber grip
his daughter bought.
Most afternoons he falls asleep in the
recliner around 2:00.
And on Tuesday, he stood up from that
recliner, took one step toward the
hallway, and watched the hallway tilt.
He sat back down, waited, and did not
mention it to anyone.
His last doctor's visit lasted 12
minutes and most of it was about his
cholesterol.
Nothing on that list made it into those
12 minutes.
There is no billing code for the things
that are going quietly wrong in a man
who says he is fine.
Everything that follows is information
for the conversation with your own
doctor, not a diagnosis of you.
Number five is the one that gets blamed
on everything except what is actually
causing it. Sleep. Howard calls it
insomnia. He has told his doctor he has
insomnia. He goes to bed at 9:00. He is
wide awake at 4:40. He is up twice in
between, and he naps in the recliner. He
has been told that is a sleep problem. A
large part of it is a timetable. Here is
what his night actually looks like. He
turns out the light at 9:00 and is
asleep in minutes because he has been
fighting his eyes since 7:30. At 1:00,
he is awake listening to the furnace. At
3:00, he is awake again and makes a trip
to the bathroom.
By 4:40, he is staring at the red
numbers on the clock doing arithmetic.
9:00 to 4:40 minus the two gaps feels
like nothing. It is more than he thinks.
Inside your brain, there is a clock, a
small cluster of cells behind the eyes
that sets the time for the whole body.
With age, that clock runs early.
Sleepiness arrives at 8:00 in the
evening instead of 11:00, and the wake
signal fires at 4:30 instead of 7:00.
Along with the earlier timetable, the
structure of the night changes. The
deepest stage, the slow-wave sleep that
makes you feel rebuilt in the morning,
shrinks.
The night gets lighter, and lighter
sleep is easier to break. So, [snorts]
you surface more often and stay awake
longer when you do.
A 2018 review in the journal Sleep
Medicine Clinics laid the whole pattern
out. With normal aging, bedtime and wake
time both move earlier, and the night
gets shorter. There are more awakenings
and more time lying awake in the dark,
more daytime naps, and less of that deep
sleep. And one detail from that review
changes how you should feel about it.
Most of the shift happens between young
adulthood and middle age. By 80, the
sleeper you have is largely the sleeper
you had at 60 with a slightly earlier
clock.
For you, that means waking at 4:40 after
a 9:00 bedtime may be close to 7 hours
of sleep. That is 7 hours in an
80-year-old body that was never going to
give you nine.
The mistake Howard makes is the mistake
most people make. He goes to bed earlier
to make up for it, which stretches the
time in bed. That spreads the same
amount of sleep thinner across more
hours. More hours in bed means more
lying awake, which feels like worse
insomnia. The bed becomes a place where
he waits.
You will notice the lighter sleep in a
particular way. A car door down the
street wakes you when it never used to.
You remember your dreams more often
because you surface out of them instead
of sleeping through them.
And you notice the pull toward the
recliner around two.
That is not weakness. It is the early
clock reaching the low point of its day
a few hours sooner than it used to.
There are warnings hiding inside
ordinary sleep change, and they are
worth knowing cold.
Loud snoring that stops and restarts
with a gasp. Waking with a headache or a
dry, raw throat.
Falling asleep in the middle of a
conversation, not just in a quiet chair
after lunch. Kicking, punching, or
shouting while dreaming. Hard enough to
wake you or to bruise.
New confusion in the evening that was
not there in the morning.
Any one of those is a reason to make
sleep the first item at your next
appointment rather than the thing you
mention at the door.
They may point to breathing that is
being interrupted or to something going
on in the brain that a simple timetable
does not explain. If you sleep alone, as
Howard [clears throat] does, nobody
hears the snoring. So ask the grandchild
who last stayed over whether you stopped
breathing or shouted in the night,
people remember that and they rarely
bring it up on their own.
Those deep hours are also when the brain
files the day away and they thin further
in people whose memory has started to
slip. So, the habit protects more than
your mornings.
One fixed wake time every day, including
Sunday, and 10 to 20 minutes of outdoor
light within an hour of it. Not light
through a window, real daylight. On the
porch with the coffee if you like. A
cloudy morning still counts because even
gray daylight is many times brighter
than any lamp in your house.
If the step is icy, stand in the open
doorway with your coat on.
Morning light is the strongest signal
the clock receives and it pushes bedtime
later so the night consolidates.
Keep the nap, but cap it at 20 minutes
and keep it before 2:00 in the
afternoon.
Set a kitchen timer before you sit down
because the recliner nap that runs to an
hour steals from the night. And stop
going to bed before you are sleepy.
For Howard, that means finding something
to do between 8:00 and 9:30 that is not
the recliner in the dark. A lamp on, a
crossword, a phone call to his daughter.
If you are awake in the dark for more
than what feels like 20 minutes, get up.
Sit in a dim chair with something dull
and go back when your eyes are heavy. Do
not check the clock when you wake and
turn it to face the wall if you have to.
The arithmetic is what keeps you up, not
the waking.
Give the new wake time two full weeks
before you judge it. The first few
mornings will feel worse because you are
getting up at the same time on less
sleep. By the second week, the sleep
starts to gather into one block. The bed
has to mean sleep again.
Howard's doctor, when he said insomnia,
offered him something to take at night.
Hold that thought. It belongs to a later
number on this list and it is going to
matter more than Howard knows. Number
four is the one you can see happening in
the mirror and still not understand.
Muscle.
Elaine is 81 and Elaine is the one who
noticed. She has been on the stairs in
her house for 40 years. Sometime in the
last two, she started putting her hand
on the rail, then both hands.
Then she started counting the trips, so
she makes one in the morning and one at
night.
The loss happened so evenly that no
single week felt different.
Once she started looking, she noticed it
in other places. The car seat sits low,
and getting out of it had become a
two-step process.
Legs out first, then a push on the door
frame.
The gallon of milk moved from the top
shelf of the refrigerator to the door,
where it was easier to lift. She had
been quietly rearranging her life around
the loss without ever naming it.
The word for it is sarcopenia, the
age-related loss of muscle tissue and
strength, and it is going on in
everybody past about 50.
What changes in the 80s is the pace. The
loss accelerates, and it is not even.
The fast-twitch fibers go first, the
ones that fire in a fraction of a second
when you catch yourself on a curb.
The nerves that drive those fibers drop
out, so the brain's signal arrives at
fewer fibers than before.
At the same time, the muscle you have
becomes harder of hearing. It needs a
bigger protein signal and a bigger
loading signal to respond with the same
amount of building.
A meal that would have kept your thighs
at 60 does not quite keep them at 82.
You will feel the fast fibers going
before you feel anything else. Your
walking is fine, but the quick step
sideways when the dog cuts in front of
you arrives late. You can carry the
laundry basket, but you cannot catch a
cup that slips off the counter.
That is the gap between strength and
speed. It is speed that keeps you off
the floor.
Ordinary is a little less grip, a little
slower on the hill, a jar that needs a
towel.
Warning is different. Needing your hands
to get out of a chair. A fall in the
last year, even one you walked away
from.
Clothes that fit loose when you have not
been trying to lose weight.
Those are the signs that the muscle loss
has reached the point where it decides
what you can do.
You can measure your own pace in the
next minute. Sit in a sturdy chair with
no arms or a kitchen chair pushed
against the wall.
Cross your arms over your chest. Stand
all the way up and sit all the way down
five [snorts] times as quickly as you
safely can.
Notice two things. Whether you could do
it at all without uncrossing your arms
and how it felt compared with the last
time you did anything like it.
Maybe five took you noticeably longer
than you would have guessed. Maybe your
hands came down to the thighs on their
own.
That is the exact thing to describe to
your doctor in those words because it
tells them more than any number on a
scale.
Elaine's first try was slow and she
stopped at four.
She wrote the number on the calendar
anyway.
That is the other use of the test. It
gives you a mark to beat.
The guidance for adults from the NIH is
150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity
a week spread across the days.
Federal health officials published their
own version aimed at older adults.
For many people in their 80s, that
number sounds like it belongs to someone
else. So, start where Elaine started.
Five chair stands twice a day, morning
and evening, holding the counter if you
need to at first. Add one every week.
Here is how to do one well. Scoot to the
front edge of the seat with your feet
flat and slightly behind your knees.
Lean your nose forward over your toes,
then push through your heels until you
are fully upright.
Lower yourself over a slow count of
three and touch down lightly instead of
dropping.
The slow sit is half the exercise, so do
not skip it. Pair it with something you
already do twice a day like brushing
your teeth and it stops needing
willpower. Nothing in a gym rebuilds the
fast fibers that catch you on a curb
better than standing up out of a chair
against gravity. That is the movement
you are training for.
And feed the muscle.
For most people, that means protein at
breakfast rather than saving it all for
dinner. An egg or two, Greek yogurt,
cottage cheese, something with substance
before 10:00 in the morning. The muscle
can only use so much at a time, and most
people after 80 give it almost nothing
until evening.
Howard's breakfast is coffee. Elaine's
used to be toast and jam, which is
almost no protein at all.
Now she has two scrambled eggs, and on
days she does not feel like cooking, a
cup of cottage cheese with fruit.
The change is small enough to keep and
large enough to matter.
If your doctor has put you on a protein
limit for your kidneys, that limit comes
first. So ask what your number is.
Elaine's rail is still on the stairs.
Three months after she started with the
chair, she uses one hand instead of two,
and she has stopped counting the trips.
Number three is the one that is almost
impossible to notice from the inside,
which is why it is on this list at all.
Thirst. [snorts]
Go back to Howard's morning. Two cups of
coffee and then nothing until lunch. If
you asked him whether he was thirsty, he
would say no, and he would be telling
the truth. That is the problem. The
thirst signal is generated deep in the
brain in response to the blood getting
slightly more concentrated. That signal
gets quieter with age.
The same loss of water that would have
had you reaching for a glass at 40
produces no message at all at 80.
Two other things are happening
underneath. The body holds less water
overall because muscle holds water, and
you have less muscle. So the same loss
is a bigger share of what you have.
And the kidneys get less skilled at
concentrating urine, so they keep
letting water go even when the body is
short of it.
There is a fourth thing, and it is not
in the body at all.
Howard does not drink in the afternoon
because he does not want to be up at
night. He He made that trade on purpose,
and he is not alone. Many people in
their 80s quietly ration water to
protect their sleep or to avoid hunting
for a restroom in a store.
The trade feels sensible. It is costing
more than they know.
The National Library of Medicine's own
patient page says it plainly.
Older adults are among the groups most
likely to become dehydrated, in part
because some lose their sense of thirst.
You cannot wait to feel it. By the time
an 80-year-old feels thirst, the
shortfall is already well along.
This is the first real payoff of the
five, and it is small enough to miss. A
quiet thirst does not feel like
anything. It shows up as other things. A
morning headache. Tiredness that a nap
does not fix.
Dizziness when you stand. Constipation
that arrived from nowhere.
And the one that frightens families, a
sudden confusion that gets labeled as a
bladder infection or as the beginning of
dementia.
It often clears within a day or two once
fluid goes in.
Howard has had the morning headache for
a year. He takes a pain reliever for it
most days, and that is one of the
bottles in his cabinet. The headache
arrives after a night of breathing out
moisture and a morning of coffee.
It is the quiet thirst speaking the only
way it still can.
The Cleveland Clinic lists the signs
worth checking yourself for.
Urine that is dark yellow and
strong-smelling.
Going to the bathroom less often than
usual. A dry mouth. Feeling light-headed
and feeling tired.
The color of your urine is the only one
of those you can read every single
morning.
Pale straw is the color you want. Look
before you flush, and look at the first
trip of the day in particular.
That one is always the darkest, and it
tells you how the night went.
If it is the color of apple juice, the
day starts with a glass before anything
else.
Think back for a moment. How many
glasses of plain water did you drink
yesterday before noon?
Not coffee, not tea, water.
If you cannot picture a single one, you
are in the majority of people your age,
and you are not in trouble yet.
Keep that number in your head, because
it comes back twice more before we are
done.
The second time it is going to connect
to the hallway that tilted on Howard.
The habit is a schedule, because the
body has stopped giving you one.
A full glass of water with every pill
you take and with every meal.
And one on the nightstand that you
finish before your feet touch the floor.
For Howard, that alone is four glasses
he was not drinking.
If you want to see it rather than count
it, fill a pitcher in the morning and
keep it on the counter.
When the pitcher is empty, the day's
water is done.
Put the last glass with dinner, not at
bedtime, so the bathroom trips stay
early.
If a full glass is hard to face, make it
half a glass and drink it anyway.
Within a week, most people notice the
morning headache fading first, then the
afternoon tiredness.
Coffee and tea do count toward fluid,
but they are not a substitute for the
glass that goes with the pills, and you
will see why in the next number.
One exception overrides all of this.
If your doctor has you on a fluid limit
for your heart or your kidneys, that
limit wins. The question for them is
simply what your daily number is and how
to spread it. Number two is the one
Howard's seven pills are quietly arguing
about every morning. Medication.
Every one of those seven was prescribed
for a reason, and most of them were
prescribed to a younger man. The dose of
a blood pressure pill that fit Howard at
68 was worked out for a different body.
That body had bigger kidneys, a bigger
liver, more water, and less fat. All
four of those have changed, and each
change pushes in the same direction.
The kidneys clear most drugs more
slowly, so each dose is still partly in
the blood when the next one arrives. The
liver is smaller and slower, so drugs
that are broken down there last longer.
There is less water in the body, which
is your number from a moment ago. So, a
drug that dissolves in water is
dissolved in less of it and runs more
concentrated. And there is more fat, so
a drug that stores in fat lingers for
days. On top of all that, the brain in
the 80s is more sensitive to anything
that sedates it. A pill that made you
pleasantly drowsy at 55 can leave you
foggy and unsteady until noon at 83.
Think of it like a sink with a slow
drain. At 60, the drain kept up and each
dose washed through before the next one
came. At 83, the drain is narrower. The
same tap, run on the same schedule,
leaves the sink a little fuller every
morning. Same tap, same schedule, only
the drain is narrower now. That pill
Howard's doctor offered for his insomnia
is in that category. He took it for 3
weeks. He slept a little longer and he
was foggier at 10:00 in the morning than
he had ever been.
He could not say why his balance felt
off in the kitchen. Nobody connected the
fog to the pill because the fog looked
like age. In the second week, he read
the same paragraph of the newspaper
three times. He put the milk in the
cupboard and found it that evening. His
daughter noticed on the phone that he
was slower to answer and she wondered
quietly if this was the start of
something.
It was the start of something. It was
the start of the pill.
Researchers who looked at nearly 1,400
older adults in Berlin asked how many
were taking a medicine considered a poor
fit for an older body. They found it was
common and the pattern was simple. The
more pills a person took, the more
likely one of them was potentially
inappropriate. The researchers tied it
directly to the way an aging body
handles and responds to drugs.
For you, that means the number on your
pill organizer is itself a risk factor,
separate from any single pill in it.
There is a trap inside this that is
worth naming once. A pill causes a side
effect, say dizziness or a new tremor or
a new bladder problem.
The side effect is read as a new
condition. A new pill is added for the
new condition and that pill brings its
own side effect. Doctors call it a
prescribing cascade and it is how seven
pills become nine without anyone ever
being wrong at any single step.
Howard's headache pill is a small
example. The headache came from the
quiet thirst. The pill went in for the
headache and nobody asked where the
headache came from. One cause, one extra
bottle.
The warnings are all the word new. New
confusion, new dizziness, a new fall,
new incontinence, new fog in the
morning.
Any of those arriving within weeks of a
new prescription or a changed dose
should be reported in that exact form.
This started after that.
Write the date you started a pill on the
lid with a marker.
Then when something new appears, you are
not guessing whether it was 3 weeks ago
or 3 months.
And in the other direction, a pill you
have taken for 15 years without trouble
can start causing trouble at 80.
The reasons are the ones above. A long
history with a drug is not a guarantee.
The habit is once a year and it takes a
brown paper bag. Put every bottle in it.
The prescriptions, the over-the-counter
sleep aid, the allergy tablet, the pain
reliever, the fish oil, the vitamin D,
all of it. Check the bathroom cabinet,
the kitchen drawer, the bedside table
and the glove box. Pills scatter in a
house and the ones in the drawer count
just as much as the ones in the
organizer. Bring the bag to a visit that
is about nothing else or bring it to
your pharmacist who can do this well and
often has more time.
Tip the bag out on the counter and go
through them one at a time. Ask two
questions about every item. Is this dose
still right for my kidneys and my body
at this age? And is this one still
earning its place or is it treating a
side effect of something else in the
bag.
Ask one more about anything you take for
sleep, allergies, or nervous bladder.
Does this one slow the brain?
Those three categories are where the fog
most often hides.
Do not stop anything on your own because
several of these can hurt you more
coming off suddenly than staying on.
But do get every one of them looked at
by someone who is seeing the whole bag
at once.
Howard's brown bag had eight things in
it, not seven, because he had never
counted the sleep pill. It was the first
thing to come out.
Number one is the one you felt in the
first sentence of this video, and it is
where all four of the others meet.
Blood pressure that is slow to follow
you when you stand.
If you said straight up a few minutes
ago, this is your number, and it is time
to tell you what it means.
When you stand, gravity pulls a share of
your blood down into your legs and
belly.
For an instant, less of it is reaching
your head. At 30, you never felt that
instant. There are sensors in the walls
of the big arteries in your neck that
read the drop. They fire a correction
within a heartbeat or two. The heart
speeds up, the vessels in the legs
tighten, and the pressure at the brain
is restored before you have finished
rising.
That system is called the baroreflex.
In the '80s, it is slower and duller,
and the main reason is the arteries
themselves.
The big vessels stiffen with age, and a
stiff artery does two things. It pushes
the top number of your blood pressure
up, and it stops stretching with each
change in pressure, so the sensors in
its wall have less to read. The alarm
still works. It just rings late and
quiet.
Picture a garden hose next to a length
of copper pipe. Squeeze the hose, and it
gives, and you can feel the water move
inside it. Squeeze the pipe, and nothing
happens.
The sensors in your neck are built to
feel the give. The artery around them
has become the pipe. That late alarm is
the half second in the kitchen. It has a
clinical name, orthostatic hypotension,
a drop in blood pressure on standing.
The usual definition is the one Mayo
Clinic uses. A fall of 20 points in the
top number or 10 points in the bottom
number within 3 minutes of standing up.
The symptoms it lists are the ones you
already know, light-headedness, blurred
vision, weakness, confusion, a feeling
of fainting, and in some people, nausea
or an ache across the shoulders. Many
people in their 80s have the drop with
no symptom at all, which is why the
measurement matters more than how you
feel. You will notice it in particular
places, getting up from the toilet,
standing after kneeling in the garden,
or bending to tie a shoe, rising from a
hot bath when the warm water has already
opened the vessels in your skin, and the
first step out of a car after a long
drive. Each of those is a sudden demand
on a reflex that now needs a moment.
Now, watch the other four changes walk
into this room. Howard's quiet thirst
means less water in his blood, so there
is less volume to begin with when he
stands. That is your water number from
earlier, connecting exactly where it was
promised. His blood pressure pills,
dosed for a younger man, pull the
pressure down further and blunt the
correction. The sleeping pills slowed
his reactions and softened his balance.
And the muscle he lost from his calves
and thighs was the muscle that squeezes
blood back up out of the legs. It does
that with every step. All five of them
were in that recliner with him. He had
slept badly and taken the pill.
He had drunk two coffees and nothing
since.
He had sat for an hour, so the blood had
settled in his legs. His calves, thinner
than last year, had less to push back
with when he stood.
None of it would have mattered at 60. At
83, it was the hallway. In 2021,
researchers from the Irish Longitudinal
Study on Aging published a look at about
1,500 adults over 65.
It found something that will sound
backwards. The drop on standing very
often lives in the same person as high
blood pressure while sitting or lying
down. The researchers tied both to the
same stiffening of the arteries and the
same dull reflex. For you, the lesson is
direct. A high reading at your visit and
a tilting hallway at home are not two
separate problems that cancel out. They
are the same artery measured in two
positions. Treating the high number
harder without checking the standing
number can make the hallway worse.
Federal health officials keep the count
of how many older Americans fall each
year. Whole prevention programs are
built on that number.
The National Institute on Aging, in its
guidance on falls and fractures, is
clear that a fall is rarely caused by
one thing.
The drop on standing is one of the
causes that almost never gets measured.
Blood pressure in the office is taken
sitting down.
It is also the one you can bring to the
appointment yourself. So, ask for it. At
your next visit, ask for your pressure
lying down after 5 minutes, then
standing at 1 minute, and again at 3
minutes. Three readings, 5 minutes.
If you have an automatic cuff of your
own, you can do it at home.
Do it in the morning before your pills
with someone else in the room the first
time.
Lie on the bed with the cuff on and read
the number after 5 quiet minutes. Then
stand beside the bed with a hand on the
nightstand and read it again at 1
minute. Stay standing and read it at
three.
If you feel faint at any point, sit down
and write that down, too.
The symptom is a reading in itself.
Write the three numbers in a row. Label
them. Lying, standing 1 minute, standing
3 minutes.
Do it on three different mornings
because the drop is not the same every
day.
A drop of 20 on the top or 10 on the
bottom is the main item of the visit. So
is any symptom while you stand there.
Not the thing you mention on the way
out.
And the habit, the one that changes
tomorrow morning. Sit on the edge of the
bed before you stand. Drink the glass of
water you left on the nightstand.
Pump your ankles up and down 10 times
and squeeze your fists.
That pushes the pooled blood back up
toward your heart before you ask your
legs to carry you.
Then stand with a hand on the headboard
or the nightstand. Count to 30 before
you take the first step. 30 seconds and
the reflex that used to take a quarter
of a second has caught up.
30 seconds is longer than it sounds. So,
count out loud the first week until your
body learns the pause.
If the room moves anyway, sit back down
and start [clears throat] the count
again. Do not try to walk through it.
Do the same count after a big meal.
Digestion pulls blood toward the gut.
The drop after lunch can be steeper than
the one at dawn.
It is also steeper in the heat, after a
hot shower, and after a glass of wine.
Those are the afternoons to sit a moment
longer.
And carry the habit to the recliner,
which is where Howard's hallway tilted.
Any chair you have been in for an hour
deserves the same ankle pumps in the
same hand on the arm.
If you said straight up, that is the
answer you came for. If you said sit,
you have been doing the right thing
without a reason. Now you have the
reason.
Six weeks after the hallway tilted,
Howard still wakes at 4:40.
He has stopped calling it insomnia.
He drinks the glass on the nightstand,
pumps his ankles, and stands with a hand
on the dresser. He counts. He takes his
coffee on the back step in the first
light. There are seven things in his
pill organizer again. The sleep pill is
gone.
One blood pressure dose was lowered
after his doctor measured him standing
and found a drop of 24 points.
He does his chair stands at the kitchen
table twice a day.
He can open the pickles with the towel.
The hallway holds still.
For the routine visit, bring the brown
bag and ask for the lying and standing
readings.
This week, do the five chair stands, put
the glass on the nightstand, and get
outside in the morning light. A faint, a
fall that strikes your head, especially
on a blood thinner, chest pain, a weak
face or arm, slurred speech. That is
911, not a note for next time.
Everything else here is a pattern from
the research applied to a composite. The
version that applies to you belongs with
your own doctor. So, take it to them in
those words. Tonight, before you turn
out the light, put a full glass of water
where your hand will find it in the
dark. You already know your new answer
for tomorrow morning. Send this to the
one person in your family who still
insists they just got up too fast. And
tell me in the comments where the room
last slid on you. The kitchen chair, the
recliner, the edge of the tub, or the
first step out of the car. Just the
place, one line. And if you want the
next change explained before it finds
you, subscribe.
Tomorrow, when the dark is still in the
window, sit on the edge of the bed,
count to 30, let the room come to you.

records.title: 4 Foods Stiffening Your Arteries After 60 — 5 That Keep Them Soft
records.location: Dr. Vitalis — Senior Health Podcast: Heart, Blood Pressure & Strong Legs After 60
records.channelDescription:
Clear, research-backed health answers for adults over 60.

Dr. Vitalis takes the questions older adults actually face and explains what the evidence says in plain language. Examples: a blood pressure reading that looks "normal" but isn't, legs that feel weaker on the stairs, a common pill with side effects nobody mentioned, a warning sign that's easy to blame on age.

What we cover:
• Blood pressure, heart health and stroke warning signs
• Kidneys, blood sugar and circulation
• Leg strength, balance and preventing falls
• Medications and supplements worth asking your doctor about
• Everyday food choices, without the hype

Every video ends with simple next steps: what to watch for, what to ask at your next appointment, and when to call right away.

Subscribe for the next one.

For educational purposes only. Not medical advice. Always talk with your own doctor before changing medications or treatment. If you think you're having a stroke or heart attack, call 911.

A stroke every 40 seconds in the U.S. After 60, your arteries are quietly stiffening — and 9 foods decide which way. Five keep the wall of your aorta flexible. Four turn it from rubber into pipe. Most older adults eat all four every week and never feel a thing, because a hardening artery does not hurt until the morning a hand will not close around the coffee mug.

This video names the five protective foods up front — extra-virgin olive oil, walnuts, nitrate-rich beets and leafy greens, beans, and high-cocoa dark chocolate — then the four stiffeners: processed meats, sugary drinks, refined white carbohydrates, and baked goods built on shortening and trans fat. Along the way you will learn what pulse pressure is, why a "borderline" blood pressure reading like 148 over 66 can be the real warning, how sugar bonds onto the collagen in an artery wall, and what one landmark Mediterranean-diet trial of 7,447 adults aged 55 to 80 actually found. Walter, the 71-year-old you meet at the start, is a composite drawn from the published case reports — and his table probably looks a lot like yours.

⏱ CHAPTERS
0:00 — The morning the right hand won't close
0:51 — The 82-point gap in a "borderline" reading
1:45 — All nine foods, named before the lecture
2:21 — How a rubber aorta turns into pipe
7:21 — Olive oil: what the 7,447-person trial found
10:45 — Walnuts, beets and greens (plus the warfarin caveat)
15:01 — Beans: the quiet swap for white rice
16:58 — Dark chocolate: why the cocoa number matters
19:12 — The ham sandwich hardening the wall
21:34 — Soda, white toast and the evening danish
29:14 — Four stroke signs and tonight's first move

If this made you look at tonight's dinner differently, subscribe and share it with the one person in your family who still calls sliced ham a light lunch.

⚠️ DISCLAIMER
This video is for educational purposes only and does not constitute medical advice. Nobody on this channel is a licensed physician, and the visuals are AI-generated. Walter is a composite drawn from published research, not a real patient. A wide pulse pressure or a bad week of eating is not a diagnosis. Consult your own physician before changing your diet or supplements, especially if you take warfarin or have a history of calcium oxalate kidney stones. If you or anyone near you has sudden drooping on one side of the face, weakness or numbness in one arm, slurred or confused speech, or a sudden loss of balance or vision, call 911 immediately — stroke treatment is measured in minutes.
